group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old man was evaluated late this afternoon in the orthopedic pre-admission clinic prior to next week’s scheduled right total knee arthroplasty, a procedure anticipated to last under two hours with regional anesthesia and short-term pneumatic tourniquet use; he has exhausted conservative measures for tricompartmental osteoarthritis documented on recent radiographs and wishes to return to recreational cycling by summer. He arrives walking without assistive devices, breathing comfortably, and converses easily, stating that he can mow his modest lawn and climb two flights of stairs while pushing a toolbox without stopping, but pain in the knee—not shortness of breath—limits his distance. Ten years ago he suffered an anterior-wall myocardial infarction while shoveling snow and underwent emergent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with deployment of two drug-eluting stents to the mid-left anterior descending artery; he completed cardiac rehabilitation, has had no recurrent chest pressure, syncope, or exertional diaphoresis since, and follows annually with cardiology. A treadmill echocardiographic stress test done nine months earlier for routine surveillance achieved 9 metabolic equivalents with no ischemic wall-motion abnormality, and the most recent transthoracic echocardiogram described a left ventricular ejection fraction of 58 % with normal diastolic filling and no valvular pathology. He has never required loop diuretics, has not experienced orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or ankle swelling, and has had no emergency visits for fluid overload. Diabetes mellitus type 2 was diagnosed in his early forties; despite lifestyle efforts, oral agents no longer sufficed, and for the past three years he has administered 24 units of insulin glargine each evening as well as mealtime insulin aspart dosed on a sliding scale before breakfast and supper. Portable glucometer records he brings today display pre-prandial values ranging from 110–160 mg/dL during the past week. Other medical problems include stage 3b chronic kidney disease attributed to hypertensive nephrosclerosis and contrast exposure at the time of his infarction, essential hypertension well managed with lisinopril 20 mg once daily and a long-acting beta-blocker, mixed dyslipidemia controlled with rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, and hyperuricemia for which he takes allopurinol. He quit smoking a pack per day twelve years ago, consumes two beers on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. Family history notes premature coronary disease in a brother at 54 and metabolic syndrome in both parents; no relatives are known to have undergone joint replacement. Current medications also include low-dose aspirin, omega-3 supplements, and topical diclofenac for the knee. He has no known drug allergies. Review of systems is otherwise negative for palpitations, claudication, transient vision changes, dizziness, fever, or unintentional weight loss. Vital signs in clinic: blood pressure 128/70 mm Hg in the right arm while seated, heart rate 64 beats per minute in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 14, oxygen saturation 98 % on room air, oral temperature 36.7 °C, and body mass index 29 kg/m². Neck veins are not distended, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, precordial palpation reveals a discrete point of maximal impulse in the fifth intercostal space mid-clavicular line, and auscultation discloses crisp S1 and S2 without additional sounds or murmurs. Lungs are clear to bases, abdomen is soft and nontender with no hepato-splenomegaly, and distal pulses are 2+ throughout without edema. The operative knee is enlarged with crepitus on passive flexion but no overlying erythema or warmth. Neurologic examination demonstrates intact cranial nerves, full motor strength, and normal sensation in all extremities. Pre-operative laboratories drawn two hours before the visit reveal hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, hematocrit 38 %, platelet count 242 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 7.4 × 10⁹/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL, consistent with long-standing baseline; estimated glomerular filtration rate is 30 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting glucose is 134 mg/dL, and HbA1c measured last month by his endocrinologist was 7.3 %. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained today shows normal sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute, Q-waves in V1-V3 compatible with prior infarction, and no acute ST-T segment abnormalities; corrected QT interval is 410 ms. Chest radiograph exhibits a normal cardiac silhouette and clear lung fields. The airway appears Mallampati class II with good cervical movement, and dentures will be removed prior to induction. He is instructed to continue his beta-blocker and aspirin up to and including the morning of surgery, to hold his evening statin the night before, to reduce the glargine dose by 30 % prior to midnight, and to omit rapid-acting insulin on the day of admission unless finger-stick glucose exceeds 180 mg/dL, in which case a protocolized dextrose-insulin infusion will be employed by anesthesia. The orthopedic team has discussed postoperative thromboprophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin and early mobilization; renal-adjusted dosing will be arranged. After reviewing risks of bleeding, infection, myocardial injury, renal impairment, and thromboembolism, the patient verbalizes understanding and remains keen to proceed with the joint replacement next Tuesday.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative factors:
- High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular): total knee arthroplasty is orthopedic → 0.
- Ischemic heart disease: prior anterior MI with coronary stenting qualifies despite the negative recent stress test → 1.
- History of heart failure: none documented → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA documented → 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: uses insulin glargine and aspart → 1.
- Preoperative serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: creatinine 2.4 mg/dL → 1.
Sum: 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 3.
Final answer: 3
